The Spanish, under a new commander, launched a major
amphibious offensive to retake Cavite in November 1896.
They attacked simultaneously at Binakayan and Dalahican.
The Filipino defenders — vastly outnumbered and
outgunned — held their ground using trenches, prepared
positions, and coordinated fire. The Spanish suffered
heavy casualties and withdrew. This victory, following
Imus, effectively ended Spanish attempts to reconquer
Cavite by force.
\n<Katipunero>They're here!
\n<Veteran>Look at them. In uniform. In formation. They think
this is a soldier's battle.
\n<Veteran>They do not know that we are fighting for our homes.
\n<Veteran>Don't let up! There's more of them coming!
\n<Veteran>We're pushing them back! Don't give them time to
recover!
\n<Katipunero>They're retreating! They're leaving their dead behind!
The victory at Binakayan-Dalahican was a turning point.
The Spanish did not attempt another major offensive in
Cavite. The revolution had proven it could not only win
battles — it could hold territory.

\n<Santiago Alvarez>You better hurry, the enemy can come at any second.
\n<Fisherman>Those are my boats they've dragged across the road. If
they stop one landing craft, they were worth it.
\n<Fisherman's Wife>My husband's on the beach with a bolo. I'm here with
the children, praying they don't march inland.
\n<Old Woman>I've seen ships on that horizon before. This time they
mean to land. This time we mean to stop them.
\n<Old Man>We buried the grain and moved the livestock up the hill.
If the fleet lands, they'll find nothing to feed an
army.
\n<Woman>Aguinaldo said stay calm, but the children hear the
cannon and cry. The cannon hasn't even started.
\n<Villager>We're not soldiers, any of us. But they're coming for
our homes, so we'll stand where we're told.
\n<Fisherman's Son>Papa says when the boats stop dragging, the shooting
starts. I'm supposed to help until then.
\n<Villager>The Commander told us to wait for the signal. Word is
he won't move a man until the village is clear.
\n<Woman>They're dragging the boats up the road, building a wall
of them. My sister's boat is in that pile.
\n<Elder>We've fought the sea all our lives. Now we fight the
men who came across it. Same muscles, same fear.
\n<Villager>Aguinaldo's with Alvarez's people at the far line. They
say if both hold, the Spanish can't land anywhere.
\n<Woman holding a bundle>A little rice, a little cloth, a prayer for each of the
men. That's all we can give them.
\n<Villager>The one in the fine coat—that's the General. He keeps
walking the line, telling us to trust the women and
children inland.
\n<Old Man>I gave my last rooster to the soldiers. A man can eat
weeds, but he can't fight hungry.
\n<Villager>They say the Spanish have iron ships and cannons that
reach the beach. They don't know the mud reaches higher.
\n<Woman>Every fighting man here was a farmer this morning. The
General made them soldiers in one speech.
\n<Villager>Talk to the General first. He'll read us the muster,
tell us where to stand. After that, it's up to God and
the tide.
\n<Villager>The General came through this morning—told us to dig,
told us to trust the trenches. Never heard a man talk
like that.
